\chapter{Mucha Agua --- When the Quantity Word Agrees}
\label{ch:mucha-agua}
\hlchaptermodality{259}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can decide whether a quantity word agrees or freezes.}

I can decide whether a quantity word agrees or freezes.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[mucha agua · pocos libros]{mucha agua · pocos libros — when the quantity word agrees}

\label{lesson:ES-C66-mucha-agua}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Mucho café}. And \emph{muy grande}, where the short form appeared because an adjective followed.

Now try \emph{mucho} in front of a \textbf{feminine} noun and listen to what your mouth wants.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: in front of a noun, it agrees}]
\begin{quote}
\emph{\textbf{mucha}} \emph{agua} · \emph{\textbf{muchos}} \emph{libros} · \emph{\textbf{pocas}} \emph{casas}
\end{quote}

When \emph{mucho} or \emph{poco} sits in front of a noun it is behaving like an adjective, so it does what every adjective does: it takes the gender and the number of the noun.

And \emph{agua} is the test case you already own. It takes \emph{el} for a sound reason while being feminine underneath — so it is \emph{\textbf{mucha}} \emph{agua}, never \emph{mucho agua}. The quantity word reports the real gender, exactly as the object pronoun did.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: after a verb, it freezes}]
Now move it behind a verb, where there is no noun for it to lean on:

\begin{quote}
\emph{Ella trabaja} \emph{\textbf{mucho}}. — She works a lot. \emph{Ella come} \emph{\textbf{poco}}. — She eats little.
\end{quote}

\textbf{No agreement.} Not \emph{mucha} because \emph{ella} is feminine — the word is not describing \emph{her}, it is describing the working. A verb has no gender and no number, so there is nothing to agree with, and the word freezes in its plain masculine-singular shape.

So one test decides it: \textbf{is it leaning on a noun, or on a verb?}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mucha agua}, \emph{muchos libros}, \emph{pocas casas}
  \item \emph{Ella trabaja mucho} — and notice nothing agreed
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
In front of a noun, does \emph{mucho} agree? (\textbf{Yes} — gender and number.)

And after a verb? (\textbf{No.} There is nothing there to agree with.)
\end{tcolorbox}
